title: Connectivity opens the door. Skills decide who walks through it
summary: Connectivity opens the door. Digital skills help Africa’s next generation decide what comes next.
body_markdown:
Nov 23, 2026


|


** 4 min.


[Kirsty Fitzgibbon](https://www.ericsson.com/en/blog/contributors/i-l/kirsty-fitzgibbon)


Vice President and Head of Marketing, Communications, Sustainability and Corporate Responsibility


Nov 23, 2026


|


** 4 min.


We talk a lot about coverage in the telecommunications industry. How many sites, how many people reached, how fast the network runs. Those numbers matter, and I spend a good part of my working life thinking about them. But I have come to believe they are only the first half of the story.


The second half is quieter. It plays out long after the network goes live, and it rarely makes the headlines. It is the simple question of what a person can actually do with a connection once they have one.


Nowhere is that question more alive than in Africa. The continent has the youngest population in the world, and a generation growing up with a phone in hand and real ambition for what comes next. As much of the world grapples with aging workforces, Africa will be sending millions of young people into working life every year.


I find myself thinking about that transition more and more. The people coming into working life over the next decade will also be the ones deciding what to build with the networks we are putting in place today. Many of them are still at school. The chances they get to try things out now will help shape what they can imagine doing later.


#### Who gets the chance to learn


A new site switched on. A town brought online. A coverage map filling in, year after year. I still take satisfaction in seeing that happen. It makes an immediate difference to how people keep in touch and find information. It also gives local businesses a chance to grow and reach new customers. Over time, that can strengthen the local economy and open up a wider range of opportunities for work.


For a young person interested in a digital career, the next step might be a first course in coding or a chance to work with equipment they have only read about. The demand for digital fluency across the continent is rising quickly. Access to training that reflects how those skills are used in practice has not kept pace. Who gets access to that training, and how early they get it, is one of the defining development questions of the next decade.


It is also the part of our work I care about most.


#### Putting skills within reach


For years, through Connect To Learn, teams across Ericsson have been working to close that gap across the world, including in Africa. The initiative helps connect schools and expand access to digital learning. Through Ericsson Digital Lab, young learners get hands-on experience in areas such as coding, robotics and electronics. Ericsson Educate, one of Connect To Learn’s key offerings, provides free, self-paced courses that connect academic knowledge with real-world industry applications in areas such as 5G, AI, the Internet of Things and cybersecurity.


Through the wider Connect To Learn initiative, this work has reached more than 670,000 children and young people across 47 countries. The aim is to give each one of those learners a little more choice about their future. A course can give a learner enough of a feel for a subject to decide whether to take it further. That can have a bearing on what they study or apply for next, giving them a little more say in their future.


I am often asked why a technology company spends its time on this. The honest answer is that we see how quickly the skills people need in our industry change. We can give learners a view of that from the inside and work with educators to make that knowledge useful wherever those learners decide to take it.


#### The ground is shifting under all of us


This work we do with educators is becoming more important as the demands of working life change. Just a few years ago, some of the skills we teach would have seemed relevant mainly to those people planning a technical career.


Today, we are moving quickly into a world shaped by AI, where systems increasingly reason, plan and act on our behalf, and where the line between the digital and the physical keeps blurring. That changes what it means to be ready for work in almost every field, from agriculture to healthcare to finance to the public sector.


It is easy to worry that the technology will move faster than people can learn to use it. I see an opening here, too. Some countries now building their digital foundations have fewer legacy systems to work around. They can design for what is coming rather than retrofit for what has passed. That gives students a chance to put what they’re learning into practice immediately, just as new digital systems take shape.


That is what makes me optimistic. Give young people across Africa access to the tools and training early enough, and they have time to experiment, make mistakes and work out which problems they want to solve. That is how they get to shape an AI economy on their own terms.


#### None of this happens alone


It takes operators willing to support learning in the communities they connect. Universities willing to open their doors. Local organizations who understand their own communities far better than we ever could. Governments setting the ambition and holding us all to it. Educators, nonprofits and the people who know how to put these programs into practice. When those partners come together around a shared goal, they can decide together where training is needed, what to teach and how to make it possible for learners to take part.


The effects can last well beyond the life of any one program. Skills, once built, do not switch off. They compound. One trained teacher reaches a classroom. One graduate starts a company. One connected community finds a use for the network that none of us would have designed from the outside.


I would like us to think about this work on the same timescale as we think about networks. Training needs to keep pace as technologies changes, and the partnership that make it possible take years to build. Both deserve our attention long after the headlines about coverage have moved on.


What I look forward to most is seeing what the generation now coming of age across a continent as vast and varied as Africa chooses to do with the opportunity. I am sure some of it will surprise us.
